p: Priya counted twenty three ask Anders notes in the margins of her old runbook, and wrote down eleven rules that lived only in people's heads.
The rules went into a Copilot instructions file in Lumen, reviewed like code, and Anders's Terraform rules got a file of their own.
Kraków got a shared prompt for date tests. Renata learned to give Copilot invented examples after Ken's scanner caught real looking rows she'd pasted from staging.
Anders approved the house rules after they planted the old bug in a test pull request and watched Copilot catch it.
At Sunday dinner Priya wrote her grandmother's dal on one of Asha's index cards, with both sides of the jaggery argument on it.
Then Ken asked for Monday morning. He wanted to talk about staging.
Ken Ito. Security lead. When he says staging, he's already found something.
Nora Kim. Compliance. She'll ask the same question twice if it matters.
Joyce Cho. The CTO. The board meets Thursday at ten.
Renata Vega. Junior engineer. Her fixtures prompt is the one the scanner flagged.
Devin Marsh. Engineer. Slower than he used to be, on purpose.
Anders Lindqvist. Infra on contract. His Terraform rules finally live in a file.
Monday came on time for once. Priya was up at six because she'd set an alarm for six, and her phone already had Ken's invite for eight o'clock. Staging. No description. Ken never wrote descriptions.

Asha's cards came at 6:40, while the kettle was still deciding. Across the top one, in purple: Week six. Fences. Every ER I worked in had locked doors and curtains. The trick was knowing which one you were standing behind.
At 7:05 a message came in from Tomasz in Kraków. Ken's invite says staging. Should I worry for my team, or for me? She didn't know yet, so she told him that.

An email from Joyce Cho. Subject: Thursday. The board is Thursday at ten. Elena will ask about the date bug. If there's anything else I should know before then, I'd like to hear it from you before I hear it from a board member. Joyce
She drove in with Ken's Friday message still in her head. The scanner sees pull requests. It never saw what went to Copilot before one was opened.
Asha's first card said: A curtain gives a patient privacy from the hallway. It doesn't stop the next bed from hearing. Know which one you've got.
The second card: Locking the drug room door was half the job. A good charge nurse tried the handle on the way past.
The third card: When a family gives you the history, write down who said it. It matters later.
The fourth card: Anything you said at the nurses' station, somebody heard. Know who, and how long they'll remember.
The last card: We said it a hundred times a night. If you didn't chart it, you didn't do it.
Ken had printed pages for the eight o'clock, which nobody at Halcyon did anymore. He handed one each to Priya, Nora, Joyce, and Renata. Renata took hers like it might be a summons.

Ken's page. The staging seed folder in lumen forecast, under fixtures, holds sixteen tables, and two of them, pre admissions and contacts, never went through the scrub script, which is older than both. On Thursday two pre admissions rows turned up in a prompt file with real looking dates of birth, and since he can't prove they're real, he's treating them as real. On Friday the pre admissions file was listed under References in two engineers' recent Copilot Chat threads, and no content exclusion covers the folder.

Some of Lumen was always going to sit close to patients, Ken said. The hospital files under config are unit names, bed counts, discharge rules. Cascade Valley Health's has forty units in it. That's why my October list exists. This folder was never on it, because nobody thought forecast had data in it.

Priya read the path twice. She knew it. Step fourteen of her July migration runbook: copy the staging seed into lumen-forecast/fixtures, already scrubbed. She'd written already scrubbed because the old README said so.
That folder came over in my migration, she said. Step fourteen. I copied it, and I didn't check it.
Across the table Renata put her page down flat. It was the first time since Ken handed it to her that she'd let go of it.
Ken had known. He'd waited for her to say it. Then what do we do today?

Ken adds the folder to the organization's exclusions after lunch, and the scrub goes on his list for the week, Renata's prompt file included. Nora writes two lines in her log: exclusion added Monday, scrub in progress. The rule keeps it out of Copilot. It doesn't make the rows go away. At the top of her page Renata writes exclude today, then scrub, and underlines it.
Content exclusion keeps chosen files from being used as context on Business and Enterprise, so it's the fast control while the cleanup happens.
At one Ken sent her the change before he saved it. He wanted a second reader, he said, because he'd been the only reader on the October list.

Ken's draft of the organization content exclusion. The October list stays above it, unchanged. Under it is one new entry for the lumen forecast repository: slash fixtures, slash staging seed, slash, and then a single star.
The seed folder had a contacts file at the top and a subfolder for each year since 2023. pre_admissions.csv lived in two of the year folders.

Two stars. One only gets the files at the top of the folder. Ken adds the second star and reads the line back to her under his breath, the way you read back an order. He saves it at 1:20. One star, the folder. Two, everything under it. His name and the time show up at the bottom of the settings page. Priya asks him to leave the October list exactly as it is, comments and all. He'd already planned to.

The paths are fnmatch patterns, and case doesn't matter. One star gets you the files sitting in that folder. Two gets every file in it or under it. At the organization level you write the repository's name, then its paths beneath.
At 1:35 Devin sent her a screen recording, forty seconds long.

In it he opened fixtures/staging-seed/contacts.csv to start on Ken's scrub list, typed a comma at the end of a row, and gray text filled in the rest of it. That's somebody's phone number shape, he said in the recording, quieter.
In the corner of the recording, the yellow page that said Careful was still taped under his monitor.
Ken had saved the rule fifteen minutes earlier. Devin's VS Code had been open since eight.
Ken's rule is in. This file still gets suggestions. Is the fence broken, or is it me? I'm asking before I decide.

He runs Developer: Reload Window from the Command Palette. When the window comes back, the Copilot icon in the status bar has a line through it, and the tooltip names Halcyon's organization settings. The gray text is gone. So it wasn't broken. It just hadn't heard yet. He types the next row of the scrub list by hand.

After a content exclusion changes, an IDE that already loaded the settings can take up to 30 minutes to pick it up. In VS Code, Developer: Reload Window applies it now. In an excluded file the Copilot icon shows a diagonal line, and its tooltip says which settings applied.
Tuesday morning Renata posted a question in the rollout channel. Nobody answered it. Six people reacted with the eyes emoji, which wasn't an answer either.
At eleven she came to Priya's desk with her laptop open. I said it in the channel. I'm saying it again here.
The second time, Priya thought. She stopped typing.

Renata had been writing a test in calculateWindow.test.ts, which nobody had excluded. Copilot had suggested a fixture with a field called preAdmitSurgeryTime. That name existed in one place in the repository: a types file in the seed folder.
The folder's excluded. So how does it know the name?

They read the limitation together. The IDE can hand Copilot semantic details from an excluded file, like types and hover definitions. A field name isn't a patient. A row is. The rule narrows what goes out. Getting the real rows out is what makes it safe. Renata writes that down, then looks up. Nobody answered me in the channel. I know. You came anyway.

The IDE can hand Copilot details from an excluded file on its own, like types, hover definitions, and build settings. That's a documented limit. Exclusion reduces exposure. Removing the sensitive data closes it.
Wednesday at 7:10 Tomasz called with his camera on. It was after three in the afternoon in Kraków, and his coffee had gone cold beside him.

One of my engineers used agent mode in VS Code yesterday to move our fixtures to the new shape. All of them. It changed eleven files in the seed folder, the year folders too. Ken's scanner flagged the pull request an hour ago. The folder is excluded. How did the agent get in?

Ken's guide had said since October: no agent mode in excluded repositories. Everyone had read that as the hospital config. The seed folder had only been excluded since Monday, and nobody had told Kraków the line reached it now.

Exclusions don't apply to agent mode or edit mode in VS Code. It isn't a setting. It's a documented limit. Tomasz closes the pull request himself and posts the rule in Polish and English: no agent mode on excluded paths until the seed is clean. Ken adds the same line to the guide and dates it. So the fence is for some of Copilot. For now. We read the list again when the docs change.

Content exclusion isn't supported in the Edit and Agent modes of Copilot Chat in VS Code. When a control has a known gap, cover it with another one, like keeping agents off those paths, and recheck the docs as support changes.
Nora came by at ten with the question she'd been writing down since Monday.

Those rows went to Copilot at least four times that we know of. Renata's prompt in VS Code last Thursday. Two chats Ken found, one of them on GitHub.com about the census job, with pre_admissions.csv in the references. And yesterday, agent mode in Kraków. Where are the rows now? Did GitHub keep them? Did it train on them? I want to write it down right the first time.

Priya pulls up GitHub's Copilot FAQ and reads the defaults with her. On Business, prompts and suggestions from IDE chat and completions aren't retained. On GitHub.com, mobile, and the CLI they're kept for 28 days. Engagement data stays two years. None of it trains GitHub's models. Nora writes it in two columns, then adds a line under both. Not kept doesn't mean not sent. No. They were sent. That's why the rows are coming out.

Those defaults are for Business and Enterprise seats. Personal plans are different: GitHub may train on them unless the user opts out. And retention only covers what's kept afterward. It can't undo what was sent.
At two Nora was back with a different question and the same notebook.
The auditors will ask when the seed folder was excluded, who did it, and what the rule said that day. Not what it says now. Ken says he saved it Monday. I need something that isn't Ken saying so.
Ken, across the table, didn't look offended. I'd want that too.

From the bottom of the Copilot settings page, Ken clicks the time of his last change and lands in the organization audit log, filtered to the event for content exclusion changes. Monday, his name, and in the details the excluded paths exactly as saved. They export the week to Nora's evidence folder, since the log keeps 180 days. And what people typed? Not in there. Never was. Nora had asked in October. She'd wanted to hear it the same way twice.

The audit log records Copilot settings changes. copilot.content_exclusion_changed shows who changed excluded paths and when, with the saved rules in its details, and the settings page links straight to it. Events are kept for 180 days, and prompts aren't included.
Thursday at 7:40 Joyce sent her the board slide with one line highlighted.
Board slide 6, draft. Since the incident: Copilot's house rules live in the Lumen repositories, reviewed like code. Copilot can no longer see patient data anywhere at Halcyon.

Under it Joyce had written: The second sentence is the one they'll remember. Is it true? My first year as a CTO, I told a board something couldn't happen. It was backups. I spent the next year taking it back. I'd rather not do that at ten this morning.

Priya read the sentence again. The true version had a folder in it, and the folder had come over on her plan. Joyce knew that. She'd been in the room Monday when Priya said it, and she was asking anyway.

They rewrite it together. The seed folder joins the October list, excluded for everyone with a Halcyon seat. Agent mode and some other surfaces don't honor exclusions, so agents stay off those paths. The real rows are being removed this week. Joyce reads it more slowly than she reads most things. It's longer. It's still true on Friday. Good. That's twice this week you told me before anybody else could.

Policies and exclusions apply on some surfaces and not others, and only to people who get Copilot from the organization. GitHub publishes which policies reach which surfaces. An honest claim names the control, its limits, and what covers the gap.
The board ended at noon. Joyce's message was one line: They asked about agent mode. It was already on the slide.
At three Anders pulled a chair up to her desk without asking.
He was writing a backup bucket module for staging, the kind of Terraform half the internet has written. Every other line filled in fine. The part he wanted never appeared.
His Terraform instructions file was open in the next tab. He'd added two rules to it since Friday.
I read the docs before I came over. Ken set the public code filter to block in October. That's what's eating it. My team wants it on allow. I said I'd ask you, because Ken would say no in one word.

Block isn't saying the code's wrong. It's saying it matches something public, checked with about a hundred and fifty characters around it, and we can't see whose or under what license. Anders thinks about that. Then he writes the block himself in twenty minutes from the provider's docs and asks Copilot Chat to check it against them. It finds a missing tag. Fine. That's useful. He says it like it costs him something, and he says it anyway.

With Block, Copilot checks suggestions plus about 150 characters of surrounding code against public code on GitHub and doesn't show matches. That guards against code with a license nobody chose. People with org seats get the org's setting.
Friday at nine Nora sent Priya a diagram for the auditors and asked her to mark it up before Ken saw it. He'll be kind about it. I'd rather be right.

Nora's draft, in five steps. Step one, the developer types in the editor, and step two, Copilot sends the prompt and the open files to GitHub. Step three, the proxy removes any excluded files from the prompt; step four, the model answers; and step five, filters check the answer, and the developer sees it.
Nora had circled step three herself, with a question mark next to it.

The editor asks GitHub for the policy first. It sends the repository's URL to ask, and GitHub says it doesn't log those. Then it builds the prompt without the excluded files. They redraw it: context gathered, minus exclusions. Prompt built. HTTPS to the proxy. Filters for manipulation, harmful content, and personal data. The model. Filters again, for content, code quality, and public code. Nora goes down it with her pen and doesn't circle anything.

Content exclusion works on the context Copilot gathers, before the prompt is built. The client gets the policy for the repository and leaves excluded content out. The proxy and filters come after, on the way to the model and back.

At two Ken's scrub merged. pre_admissions and contacts were gone, replaced with rows for people who had never existed: invented names, invented dates, three date fields and a time zone in every row, in the shape Renata had worked out the week before.
Then he pulled the week's Copilot entries from the audit log, because he always did before he closed anything.

The organization audit log, Copilot entries this week, where every content exclusion change shows as copilot dot content exclusion changed. Ken made one on Monday at 1:20. On Friday at 1:58, Ken added a Copilot Business seat.
The last line was a new engineer in Kraków who started Monday. Ken had checked that too.
Before I tell Nora it's closed, how do we know the fence holds? I'm not signing a line I haven't tested.

They follow the docs step by step. In calculateWindow.ts an edit gets a suggestion, so Copilot is working. The same edit in a seed file gets nothing, and the icon has its line through it. With only the seed file open and attached, they ask Chat to explain this file. It can't, and the file isn't in the References. Ken writes the evidence line and leaves room under his name. You copied it in. You should sign that it's out. Priya signs. Then she opens the July runbook to step fourteen, crosses out already scrubbed, and writes: checked, November 13.

To test content exclusion, confirm Copilot works in a file that isn't excluded, then make the same edit in an excluded file and expect no suggestion. For chat, attach only the excluded file and ask about it. Copilot shouldn't use it, and it shouldn't be listed in References.
At 4:30 Nora's evidence log had a new line in it, tested and signed by two people.
The staging seed was scrubbed. Not mostly.
The public code filter stayed on Block. Anders's module merged at five with a comment on its first line: written, not suggested.
Most of what she'd learned this week was where the fences didn't reach. She'd rather know that on a Friday in November than hear it from an auditor in March.
On Saturday she drove to Asha's. Asha's back gate had sagged until it wouldn't latch, and Raj had come with a drill and an opinion.
Priya held the gate while he worked and told them about step fourteen: already scrubbed, because a README said so, on a plan with her name at the top.
And who said it was yours?
Me. Monday morning, before anybody asked. Asha nodded and didn't say good, which from her meant good.

Her father set the drill down. First job they gave me with my name on the ticket, I scrapped twenty two parts. Wrong offset. I'd copied it off the last man's sheet. Foreman made me fill out the scrap tags myself. All twenty two. Same capitals I'd put on the ticket.
I kept a tag. He didn't say where. Asha did. His wallet. Since 1979.
He shut the gate and the latch caught. Then he sent Priya around to the alley side. Push it like you want in.
She put her shoulder into it. It held.
Again, he said, and she pushed again, harder, and it held again, and Asha went in to put the kettle on.
